subject: pcountOpen - problems with K in parboot?

messages.author: f4bebbdb3c5fcabc
messages.subject: pcountOpen - problems with K in parboot?
parts:
I set up a pcountOpen simulation for a horseshoe crab data set that's very sparse. The best model (as per the AIC) uses a negative binomial distribution, a trend and immigration (and a number of site and observation covariates are included). I set K to 200.

Now when I try to run parboot, at some point I get "specified K is too small. Try a value larger than any observation"
The maximum number of counts at one location is 4... Any suggestions on what is going on? I'm running it parallel on our university's HPC, FYI

Thanks!

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] pcountOpen - problems with K in parboot?
parts:
Dear Geraldine,

in your parboot, new data sets are simulated under your model, using the parameters estimated from your actual data set. Each replicate data set is then analysed using the same model, and, using the same value of K.

The error message seems to indicate that for some simulated data set, the maximum count was larger than 200. This may seem strange, but you have a NegBin distibution, which produces such extreme counts more often than the Poisson. So, you have to repeat the analysis of the actual data set with a K that is larger, such that it is large enough for ALL simulated data sets.

Different thing: Have you checked whether your estimates are stable when you increase K ? Such sensitivity of the estimates to K is a frequent problem with NegBin mixtures for the static Nmix model and I could imagine it also happens in the dynamic Nmix (i.e., Dail-Madsen).

Best regards  -- Marc

messages.author: f4bebbdb3c5fcabc
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] pcountOpen - problems with K in parboot?
parts:
Ah, of course - Thanks Marc! I thought it sampled only from the original dataset. That makes sense with the NB distribution.
Also, I looked at the estimates of the model for the separate sites (grids, in my case) and there seems to be one site/grid that goes a little "off the rails" with the exponential growth. I'll have to have a look to see what's going on there. I have a dataset with a large number of grids that have not all been sampled with the same frequency - I suspect this one might be very undersampled in comparison with others. In another project that I was working on (ticks), I noticed this created something similar.

I increased K step-wise until the results stabilized; but I'll have a look at that again, thanks.
